z-m-27-01.title: How many ways are there to hand out 6 candies?
z-m-27-01.topic: The number of ways to hand out candies: whether candies are told apart and whether empty hands are allowed
z-m-27-01.goal: Realize that the sentence 'the number of ways to hand out' alone does not fix a single answer, and rewrite the problem by stating for yourself the conditions needed to decide the answer (whether candies are told apart, whether empty hands are allowed).
z-m-27-01.material: We want to hand out all 6 candies to three people, 갑, 을, and 병. 갑, 을, and 병 have fixed names, so they are different people. Ways of handing out candies are counted by the result 'who received what.' If the result is the same, it is the same way, and the order of giving candies is not counted. The problem is just one sentence. "How many ways are there to hand out 6 candies to three people?"
z-m-27-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough before finding the answer
z-m-27-01.thinking.1: Predicting how the number of cases changes when the conditions change
z-m-27-01.thinking.2: Checking by building cases whose conditions are fixed
z-m-27-01.thinking.3: Rewriting an ambiguous problem so that it has a single answer
z-m-27-01.prereq.0: Writing the cases as ordered pairs and listing them without missing any
z-m-27-01.prereq.1: The product rule and the sum rule (level of the early part of the 'counting cases' unit in high school Common Mathematics)
z-m-27-01.prereq.2: The H2 in the school-level assignment is only a difficulty label in this production plan, not a school grade assignment. Assume the basic ideas of the counting-cases unit have already been learned.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.prompt: For this one sentence alone to have a single answer, what more must we absolutely know? Choose all that apply.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.0: Separate, as if drawing a line, the conditions already written in the problem text from the conditions that are not written.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.1: Fix one count for (갑, 을, 병) so that the result stays the same, and think about which condition, if changed, would make that result different or impossible.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.a: The ages of the three people 갑, 을, and 병
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.a: Age has nothing to do with how many ways there are to divide. Think about which information changes the way of counting.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.b: Whether the 6 candies are told apart from each other
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.b: You noticed that depending on whether the candies are told apart, even the same distribution of numbers can be counted as different ways.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.c: Whether candies are given one at a time in turn or all at once
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.c: This problem has been set up to count only the result and not the order of giving. It is already a fixed condition.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.d: Whether it is fine if one of the three people gets no candy at all
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.d: You noticed that whether the cases where someone receives 0 are included changes the very list of possible cases.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.o.e: Whether 갑, 을, and 병 are different people
z-m-27-01.s.s1.r.e: It is already written that they have fixed names. Separate the information that is given from the information that is missing.
z-m-27-01.s.s1.explain: There are two pieces of missing information. Depending on whether the candies are told apart, even when the numbers are the same, like (갑 4, 을 1, 병 1), it becomes a different way if the candies received are different. Also, the possible cases change depending on whether an empty hand is allowed. That the people are told apart and that the order of giving is not counted have already been given.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.prompt: Let's fix the case where all 6 candies are the same kind and all three people receive at least 1 each. Enter 6 different ways. (the number 갑 receives is a, the number 을 receives is b, the number 병 receives is c)
z-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the number one person receives, and look at what the sum of the numbers the other two people receive must be.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.1: Are (4,1,1) and (1,4,1) the same way? Check against the problem text's standard that 'if the result is the same, it is the same way.'
z-m-27-01.s.s2.ok.c1: All three people have 1 or more.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.fail.c1: All three people must receive at least 1 each.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.ok.c2: Candies cannot be split, so the numbers are integers.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of candies must be an integer.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the numbers the three people receive must be 6.
z-m-27-01.s.s2.explain: Under this condition there are 10 ways in all. (1,1,4), (1,4,1), and (4,1,1) are counted as different ways because the person who gets 4 candies is different. This is because the three people are told apart. Even the same group of numbers (1,2,3) splits into 6 ways depending on who receives how many.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.prompt: This time suppose the 6 candies are all of different flavors, and it is fine for a person to get none. Compared with dividing candies of the same kind with empty hands allowed (28 ways), what happens to the number of ways?
z-m-27-01.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one distribution from the same-kind case, (4,1,1), and work out directly into how many ways that distribution splits when the candies are told apart.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think of deciding, candy by candy, 'which of the three people gets it,' and count how many times that choice is repeated.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.a: It decreases. Because the candies must be told apart, the condition is stricter.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.a: Telling candies apart does not make any possible distribution disappear. Look at into how many ways the same distribution of numbers splits.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.b: It is the same, 28 ways. Because the number of candies and the number of people stay the same.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.b: Even if the numbers of candies and people are the same, in the same (4,1,1) distribution it is a different way if who gets which candies is different.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.c: It increases. Because one distribution splits into several ways.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.c: You pointed out that once candies are told apart, one distribution breaks into several ways.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.o.d: We cannot know without working out what happens.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.r.d: You can compare the sizes without calculating everything, by looking at just one distribution and how many ways it splits into.
z-m-27-01.s.s3.explain: If the candies are all different, each candy chooses one of three people, so it is 3 to the 6th power, that is, 729 ways. That is far more than the 28 ways for the same kind. This is because each of the 28 splits into several ways. For example, even (4,1,1) alone splits into many depending on which 4 candies 갑 receives.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.prompt: Revise the first sentence and write the problem in two different interpretations so that each has one answer. You do not have to find the answers (how many ways), but write them so that it is clear which conditions you added.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.hint.0: Fix the two pieces of missing information you chose at first, one at a time, and put them into the sentence.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.hint.1: The two interpretations must differ in at least one condition. Decide which condition to change and write it.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Can you say in one line what condition differs between the two interpretations you wrote?
z-m-27-01.s.s4.selfAssess.1: When you read each interpretation, can you tell whether the candies are the same or told apart?
z-m-27-01.s.s4.selfAssess.2: In each interpretation, can you tell whether it is fine for someone to receive no candy?
z-m-27-01.s.s4.model.0: Interpretation 1) All 6 candies are the same kind, and it is fine for a person to receive 0. Interpretation 2) All 6 candies are different flavors, and it is fine for a person to receive none.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.model.1: It can be written as the number of ways to divide 6 identical candies so that all three people get at least 1 each, or as the number of ways to divide 6 candies that are told apart so that no one is left out.
z-m-27-01.s.s4.modelNote.1: This answer chose the third combination of conditions (told apart + everyone gets 1 or more). Even if the combination differs, it is valid as long as the conditions are clear.

z-m-27-02.title: Are there 36 even numbers made with the card that has 0 on it?
z-m-27-02.topic: The number of three-digit even numbers made with a card that has 0
z-m-27-02.goal: Realize that the number of choices for each place can depend on earlier choices, check and fix the solution, and confirm the answer with a different solution.
z-m-27-02.material: There are 5 cards with 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 written on them, one number each. Choose 3 different cards from them and line them up in a row to make a three-digit natural number. If 0 comes first, it is not a three-digit number, so it cannot be made. The problem asks how many even numbers can be made this way. Minseo's solution is as follows. "1) The ones place is one of the even cards 0, 2, 4, so 3 ways. 2) The hundreds place cannot use 0, so 4 ways. 3) The tens place is one of the remaining 3 cards, so 3 ways. 4) 3×4×3=36, so 36."
z-m-27-02.thinking.0: Examining whether the solution holds in every case
z-m-27-02.thinking.1: Adjusting confidence in the solution after seeing new data
z-m-27-02.thinking.2: Confirming the same answer with different solutions
z-m-27-02.prereq.0: The product rule and the sum rule (level of the early part of the 'counting cases' unit in high school Common Mathematics)
z-m-27-02.prereq.1: Lining up different cards in a row to make three-digit numbers (the ideas of hundreds, tens, and ones places)
z-m-27-02.prereq.2: The H2 in the school-level assignment is only a difficulty label in this production plan, not a school grade assignment. Assume the basic ideas of the counting-cases unit have already been learned.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.prompt: Data are revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your thought about Minseo's answer 36.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.hint.0: If you doubt the '4 ways' in line 2, write down directly how the cards that can be used in the hundreds place change when the card placed in the ones place changes.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.hint.1: In the revealed data, group the numbers with the same ones digit and count them, and match them one by one with each number in 3×4×3.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Minseo multiplied the numbers of choices for the ones place, the hundreds place, and the tens place in turn.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you see Minseo's solution now?
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.after: As a first impression, it is natural to think 36 is right because multiplying is a common way to solve. But it is too early to be sure until you check whether the '4 ways' in line 2 depends on the card in the ones place.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It was a solution that multiplied the numbers of choices place by place in turn, so 36 seems right.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The multiplying method itself is often right. But we have not yet checked whether the number of choices in the later places changes with the earlier choices.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There are 5 cards, so 5×4×3=60 seems right.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You have to consider both the case where 0 comes first and the even-number condition. 60 is a value that ignores both conditions.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I want to check whether the hundreds place's '4 ways' is always 4 ways.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is the thought of checking whether the choice at an earlier step changes the number of choices at a later step.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: From the solution alone, I can't expect any value, so I put off my judgment.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: If you decide which line of the solution to doubt, you can check it directly. There is no need yet to give up on judging.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.info: I wrote out directly all the three-digit even numbers with 2 in the ones place: 102, 132, 142, 302, 312, 342, 402, 412, 432, which is 9. The numbers that came in the hundreds place are 1, 3, and 4.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing this data, how does your thought about 36 change?
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.after: There is now evidence that Minseo's solution does not hold in every case. When it is 2, the hundreds place cannot use 0 and also cannot use the 2 placed in the ones place, so there are 3 ways. Asserting that 36 is wrong, or saying you will check the other cases too, are both reasonable.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: When it is 2, the hundreds place has only 3 ways, so 36 is hard to trust.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You confirmed, from the data written out directly, that an earlier choice changes the number of later choices.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I only looked at the case of 2, so until I see the cases of 0 and 4, I can't know whether 36 is true or false.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a careful judgment that does not decide the whole from only some cases. But you have already obtained evidence that one step of the solution is wrong.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Only the case of 2 is special, so 36 is right as it is.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: If the '4 ways' was wrong when it is 2, the multiplication solution already does not hold. Think about whether it is the same when it is 4.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: There are 9, so multiplying by the 3 ways for the ones place gives 27.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You did not check whether the 9 for the case of 2 can be used as it is for the cases of 0 and 4.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.2.info: For even numbers with 0 in the ones place, the hundreds place has 4 ways among 1, 2, 3, 4 and the tens place has the remaining 3 ways, so 12. For even numbers with 4 in the ones place, there are 9, in the same way as when it is 2.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many three-digit even numbers are there in all?
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.2.after: It is 12+9+9=30. The number of choices for the hundreds place differs between the case where the ones place is 0 and the other cases, so you have to split the cases and count them by the sum rule.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You treated the cases where the ones place is 0, 2, and 4 all as 9. When it is 0, there are 12.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is the same answer as Minseo's multiplication. Compare with the data that there are 12 when it is 0 and 9 each when it is 2 or 4.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You split the cases and added as 12+9+9.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You left out the case where the ones place is 4.
z-m-27-02.s.s1.reflect: Whether you trusted 36 at first or doubted it, which data changed your thought about which line of the solution? How can we tell apart the cases where we can count all at once by multiplying from the cases where we must split into cases?
z-m-27-02.s.s2.prompt: Jihu found the number of even numbers by a different method. Choose the wrong line in this solution.
z-m-27-02.s.s2.hint.0: Take the '4 ways' in line 4 and check it directly by deciding on one card placed in the ones place. Check whether that card can also come in the hundreds place.
z-m-27-02.s.s2.hint.1: Read in what order the multiplication in line 1 makes its choices, and compare it with the order in line 4.
z-m-27-02.s.s2.line.0: All three-digit numbers: 4 ways for the hundreds place (excluding 0), 4 ways for the tens place, and 3 ways for the ones place, so 4×4×3=48
z-m-27-02.s.s2.line.1: A three-digit number is even or odd, so (number of even numbers)=48-(number of odd numbers)
z-m-27-02.s.s2.line.2: An odd number has 1 or 3 in the ones place, so 2 ways
z-m-27-02.s.s2.line.3: Then the hundreds place has 4 ways excluding 0, and the tens place has the remaining 3 ways
z-m-27-02.s.s2.line.4: There are 2×4×3=24 odd numbers, so there are 48-24=24 even numbers
z-m-27-02.s.s2.explain: Line 4 is wrong. When 1 or 3 is placed in the ones place, the hundreds place cannot use not only 0 but also the card used in the ones place, so there are 3 ways. Then there are 2×3×3=18 odd numbers, and 48-18=30 even numbers, the same as the earlier answer. The 48 in line 1 is right. It is the value from multiplying in turn 4 ways for the hundreds place, the remaining 4 ways for the tens place including 0, and 3 ways for the ones place.
z-m-27-02.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Minseo why her solution 36 is wrong, and suggest one way to check whether 30 is right.
z-m-27-02.s.s3.hint.0: Fix one case with 0 in the ones place and one case with 2, and write down directly the cards that can be placed in the hundreds place.
z-m-27-02.s.s3.hint.1: For the way to check, pick one different route, such as changing the order of the solution or subtracting the odd numbers from the total, and work out the numbers.
z-m-27-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write in your own words that the number of cards that can come in the hundreds place depends on the card placed in the ones place?
z-m-27-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check with numbers that the way of checking you suggested really gives 30?
z-m-27-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does your answer include both 'why it is wrong' and 'how to check'?
z-m-27-02.s.s3.model.0: If the ones place is 0, there are 4 cards for the hundreds place, 1, 2, 3, 4, but if the ones place is 2 or 4, we can't use 0 and that card, so there are 3. So you can't always multiply by '4 ways.' Split the cases and check with 12+9+9=30.
z-m-27-02.s.s3.model.1: It is right that 0 can't come first, but the even card placed in the ones place can't be used in the hundreds place either. That is left out only when 0 is placed in the ones place. By another method, subtracting the 18 odd numbers from all 48 three-digit numbers also gives 30.
z-m-27-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an answer checked by the method of subtracting from the total.
